strengths: Proposes a clear and timely reformulation of video anomaly detection as language-guided open-world detection, explicitly modeling the anomaly definition as a conditioning variable z and framing the problem as concept drift.

Introduces PreVAD, a large-scale and diverse video anomaly dataset with 35,279 videos, multi-level taxonomy, and anomaly descriptions, which is a substantial resource for weakly supervised and language-guided VAD.
Provides extensive zero-shot evaluations on seven VAD datasets and reports strong detection and classification improvements over competitive baselines such as PEL, VadCLIP, OVVAD, and LAVAD.
Includes ablation studies that support the utility of the proposed dynamic video synthesis module, contrastive loss with hard negative mining, and language guidance.
The overall writing is clear, the motivation is well illustrated, and the new benchmark protocol is potentially useful for future open-world VAD research.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling variable anomaly definitions and concept drift is insufficiently validated quantitatively: the paper mostly shows cross-dataset zero-shot results using target dataset class names as prompts, and concept drift itself is demonstrated only through qualitative examples. A benchmark where the same videos are evaluated under conflicting user definitions is missing.

The training data appear to provide only one definition/label per video, with no counterfactual examples of the same pattern being normal under one definition and abnormal under another. It is therefore unclear how the model reliably learns the intended (v,z)->y mapping rather than relying on target class-name prompts at test time.

Dataset construction uses web videos, existing video-text datasets, and foundation-model-based annotation, but the paper does not adequately address ethical/legal issues such as privacy, consent, copyright, licensing, or potential annotation bias. Data/code are only promised to be released, with no reproducibility or ethics statement.

Some experimental comparisons and tables are unclear or potentially unfair. For example, Table 4 has confusing column names/values, and comparisons to OVVAD involve different training data and AIGC augmentation. The classification F1 on UCF is lower than VadCLIP despite the claim of comprehensive improvement.

The algorithmic novelty may be incremental: the architecture is largely CLIP-based with a temporal encoder, Transformer fusion, and MIL losses, while the main new components are data augmentation and contrastive regularization. The paper does not sufficiently position this against prompt-based/open-vocabulary VAD methods.

Key implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, model size, and computational costs are relegated to the supplementary material, making the main paper less self-contained and harder to assess for reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: open-world video anomaly detection where anomaly definitions may change due to user requirements or policy updates.
Proposes a language-guided paradigm that conditions anomaly detection on user-provided natural-language definitions, which is a plausible direction beyond fixed-category open-set/open-vocabulary VAD.

Introduces LaGoVAD with two reasonable regularization strategies: dynamic video synthesis to vary anomaly duration and contrastive learning with hard negative mining to improve vision-language alignment.
Builds PreVAD, a large-scale dataset with 35,279 videos, multi-level category labels, and anomaly descriptions. If released responsibly, this could be a useful resource for the community.
Reports extensive zero-shot evaluation on seven VAD datasets and compares with several reproduced and published baselines, showing consistent detection improvements on many benchmarks.
Provides ablation studies suggesting that both dynamic video synthesis and negative mining contribute to performance.
Includes qualitative examples that illustrate how language guidance can change predictions when users redefine anomalies.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling variable anomaly definitions/concept drift is not quantitatively evaluated. The main experiments are standard zero-shot cross-dataset detection using target-dataset class names, not controlled tests where users redefine previously normal patterns as abnormal or vice versa. Thus the paper's core contribution is not directly measured.

The theoretical framing overclaims that conditioning on z 'avoids' concept drift. If the test-time distribution of definitions z differs from training, the model may still fail. No failure analysis or robustness evaluation under novel or adversarial definitions is provided.

Serious ethical and legal concerns are unaddressed. PreVAD is scraped from YouTube, web videos, government streams, violence datasets, and accident compilations, yet there is no discussion of consent, licensing, copyright, privacy, IRB review, content warnings, or safeguards such as blurring faces/license plates. Releasing such a dataset may violate platform terms and copyright.

Dataset quality and validity are under-validated. Annotation uses MLLM/VLM/LLM pipelines with limited human verification, no inter-annotator agreement, no description-quality analysis, and no bias analysis. Potential overlap or leakage with UCF-Crime and XD-Violence is not checked, despite both being web-sourced.

The 'largest and most diverse' claim is based mainly on video count. In total hours, PreVAD is comparable to XD-Violence, and the paper explicitly excludes long untrimmed videos, introducing a short-clip bias that may not reflect real-world open-world surveillance.

Technical novelty is limited. Language-conditioned detection is related to existing text-prompted/open-vocabulary VAD, dynamic video synthesis is a form of data augmentation, and hard negative contrastive learning is largely standard.

Evaluation and claims are sometimes overstated. Table 3 shows LaGoVAD has lower UCF F1 (16.64) than VadCLIP trained on PreVAD (17.81), which contradicts the claimed SOTA classification performance. No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported.

Reproducibility is weak. Important details on architecture, hyperparameters, prompts, class mappings, dataset curation, and evaluation protocols are deferred to a supplementary file that is not available for review, and no anonymous code/data link is provided.

Presentation is often unclear. There are numerous grammatical errors, confusing table formatting (e.g., Table 4), and ambiguous equations/definitions, which makes some technical claims difficult to verify.
The paper does not adequately compare with recent open-world VAD methods such as HAWK for detection, and the OVVAD comparison is limited to only a subset of datasets.

strengths: Proposes a novel and well-motivated open-world VAD paradigm that conditions anomaly detection on user-provided natural language definitions, directly addressing concept drift in anomaly definitions.
Introduces LaGoVAD with two sensible regularization strategies: dynamic video synthesis and contrastive learning with hard negative mining, supported by ablations.
Builds PreVAD, a large-scale video anomaly detection dataset with 35,279 videos, multi-level categories, and fine-grained anomaly descriptions; this is a significant resource contribution.
Provides extensive zero-shot evaluations on seven VAD datasets and reports state-of-the-art detection and classification performance, with comparisons against multiple competitive baselines.
Includes qualitative illustrations of concept drift handling and ablation studies demonstrating the value of language guidance, dynamic synthesis, and hard negative mining.
weaknesses: The core dynamic-definition/concept-drift capability is mostly evaluated through cross-dataset zero-shot transfer and qualitative examples; a direct quantitative benchmark for redefining the same or similar patterns under different user definitions is limited.

Dataset construction relies heavily on foundation models for cleaning/annotation; human verification, licensing, privacy, and broader ethical considerations for web-sourced surveillance data are not discussed in detail in the main paper.

Several technical details and equations are unclear or have notation issues, e.g., the contrastive loss denominator in L_{v->t}, repeated symbols in the dynamic video synthesis loss, and malformed/ambiguous Table 4 headers.
Prompt design for target datasets appears manual and its sensitivity is not analyzed, which may affect reproducibility and fairness of zero-shot comparisons.
The paper defers many important implementation, dataset, and evaluation details to the supplementary material, making the main paper less self-contained.

strengths: Introduces a timely and well-motivated open-world VAD setting with user-provided natural-language anomaly definitions, formalizing the problem as conditional modeling (V,Z)->Y and framing label change as concept drift.

Constructs PreVAD, a large-scale video anomaly dataset with 35,279 videos, 209.5 hours, multi-level taxonomy, and anomaly descriptions; the scalable curation pipeline combining foundation models and human annotation is a useful resource for the community.

Proposes LaGoVAD with two reasonable regularization strategies—dynamic video synthesis to diversify anomaly-duration distributions and contrastive learning with hard negative mining for better vision-language alignment—and ablations show each component contributes.
Provides extensive zero-shot evaluation across seven datasets and two protocols, with SOTA results on most metrics and qualitative examples demonstrating adaptation to dynamic definitions.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, compute requirements, and code/data release plans are sufficiently reported for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited: conditioning VAD on text prompts/definitions has been explored before, and the proposed paradigm does not deeply model uncertainty over Z or estimate P(Z|V); it mainly supplies Z at inference, which sidesteps rather than solves concept drift in a fundamental way.

PreVAD's quality is not sufficiently validated: descriptions and anomaly judgments are generated/filtered by MLLMs/LLMs, with no inter-annotator agreement, no human verification of all descriptions, and little analysis of hallucination/label noise. Ethical/copyright/privacy concerns are only briefly addressed.

Evaluation fairness and zero-shot claims need clarification: Table 2 includes rows where LaGoVAD is trained with PreVAD+XD for UCF and PreVAD+UCF for XD, which conflicts with a strict zero-shot protocol; baselines are trained with different data/supervision, making SOTA comparisons less clean.

Protocol 2, the key concept-drift evaluation, is limited to XD and MSAD and only five random category subsets; comparisons with LLM-based models may be unfair because continuous frame-level scores are converted to binary boundaries.

Dynamic video synthesis may introduce synthetic artifacts and noisy pseudo-labels, and the contrastive loss uses learned anomaly scores to aggregate features, which could reinforce early prediction errors; these risks are not theoretically or empirically analyzed.
Ablations are incomplete: no variance across runs/seeds, no systematic ablation of architecture/fusion/text encoder choices, and prompt sensitivity is only tested on UCF-Crime.

The claim of being the largest and most diverse VAD dataset is not rigorously supported by quantitative diversity metrics, and comparisons such as '35 categories vs. MSAD's 55' complicate the 'most diverse' claim.

strengths: Introduces a novel open-world VAD paradigm that models anomaly definitions as stochastic variables and conditions detection on both video and language definition, targeting concept drift.

Proposes LaGoVAD with two regularization strategies: dynamic video synthesis for diversifying anomaly durations and contrastive learning with hard negative mining for robust vision-language alignment.

Builds PreVAD, a large-scale video anomaly dataset (35,279 videos, 209.5 hours, 7 top-level and 35 subcategories) with multi-level annotations and anomaly descriptions, which is a potentially valuable resource.
Provides extensive zero-shot evaluation across seven datasets under two protocols, including concept drift evaluation, plus ablations on dataset, architecture, and loss components.
Includes detailed implementation, data curation pipeline, prompts, and reproducibility materials, with code and dataset promised for release.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: language-guided VAD and conditioning on text definitions are incremental over existing open-vocabulary VAD and prompt-based methods; the method mostly combines CLIP encoders, temporal attention, MIL losses, and standard contrastive learning.

Evaluation comparisons are not fully controlled: baselines in Table 2 are trained on different datasets and supervision regimes, making SOTA claims difficult to verify. Protocol 2 is only evaluated on XD and MSAD, not all seven datasets.

Concept drift improvements are modest and not consistently strong, e.g., on MSAD drift@5 LaGoVAD AUC is 0.856 vs VadCLIP 0.852, and classification F1 on UCF is lower than VadCLIP trained on PreVAD (16.64 vs 17.81), contradicting claims of consistent improvement.

The dataset quality is not rigorously validated: PreVAD's anomaly descriptions are MLLM-generated, with human verification limited to category labels and a validation subset; normal videos from generic video-text datasets may not match target-domain normal distributions, and no independent human evaluation of description accuracy is provided.

Method details are unclear, especially how the anomaly definition z is constructed during training, how random definitions are sampled within a batch, and how the language-guided branch exactly affects binary detection versus the language-agnostic branch. Some tables are difficult to parse and contain typos.

Claims such as 'avoid concept drift' are overstated: the model still requires the test-time definition z and therefore assumes access to the changed definition, which sidesteps rather than eliminates the underlying distribution shift.

Reproducibility and ethical issues remain: the dataset is sourced from web, streaming, and movie-like sources with potential copyright/privacy concerns, and release of code/data is only promised, not available at review time.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a timely open-world VAD setting where anomaly definitions can change at inference and are guided by natural language; the concept-drift formulation P(Y|V) vs. P(Y|V,Z) is clear and well motivated.

Constructs PreVAD, a large-scale and diverse video anomaly dataset (35,279 videos) with hierarchical categories and anomaly descriptions; this is a significant resource for weakly supervised and open-world VAD research.

Proposes LaGoVAD with two well-motivated regularization strategies: dynamic video synthesis for duration diversity and contrastive learning with hard negative mining; ablations show both components contribute.

Provides extensive zero-shot evaluation on seven datasets under two protocols, including cross-domain detection/classification and concept-drift-specific evaluation; results are generally state-of-the-art against diverse baselines.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and training setup are sufficiently described, and the paper promises code and dataset release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The model architecture is relatively simple, relying on CLIP features and a Transformer fusion module; the core technical novelty is moderate, with the main contributions being the task formulation and dataset rather than a fundamentally new detection architecture.

The language-guided open-world claim is not stress-tested with truly arbitrary or novel anomaly definitions beyond dataset category names and curated prompts; the drift protocol mainly redefines subsets of existing categories, so prompt compliance and generalization to unseen semantic definitions remain underexplored.

Dataset quality relies on MLLM/LLM automated annotation; despite human verification of categories, descriptions may contain hallucinations or annotation bias, and only the validation set has frame-level labels. Potential overlap/contamination with benchmark test sets is not thoroughly analyzed.

Some comparisons and table entries mix training sets (e.g., PreVAD+XD, PreVAD+UCF), and Protocol 2 compares a model trained on large-scale PreVAD against largely training-free or not-fine-tuned LLM baselines, which may not fully isolate the effect of language guidance under concept drift.

The main-text ablation table is formatting/alignment-wise confusing, and several claims are stronger than the evidence on some datasets where gains are modest; ethical/privacy considerations around web/streaming data are briefly stated but could be more detailed.
